title: Size it from the stop
description: An account, a risk fraction and a stop distance. How many shares?
context: Account 25,000. You risk one per cent of it on this trade. Your stop sits 0.80 away from the entry.

options.text: 195 shares
312 shares
500 shares
It depends on the win rate

explanation: One per cent of 25,000 is 250, and 250 divided by 0.80 is 312.5, so 312 whole shares. The win rate does not enter: size comes from the money you will risk and the distance to the stop, and nothing else. Lesson 20 is the arithmetic and lesson 21 is where the 0.80 comes from.

title: Expectancy on four numbers
description: A win rate and two averages. Is the method positive?
context: Over a long record: 40 per cent of trades win, the average winner is 2.2R and the average loser is 1R.

options.text: Negative, because it loses more often than it wins
+0.28R a trade
+0.88R a trade
Break-even

explanation: Expectancy is 0.40 times 2.2 less 0.60 times 1.0, which is 0.88 minus 0.60 and comes to +0.28R a trade. Answer C is the winning half on its own, which is the mistake the calculation exists to prevent: a win rate under half says nothing by itself. Lesson 17.

title: How much is open at once
description: Five positions, one risk fraction. What is at stake if they all stop together?
context: You hold five positions and each risks one and a half per cent of the account.

options.text: 1.5 per cent, because only one will stop
3.0 per cent
7.5 per cent
Cannot be known without the correlations

explanation: Portfolio heat is positions times risk per trade: five times 1.5 is 7.5 per cent. That is the day every stop hits at once, and it is the day the limit exists to survive. Correlation changes how often that day arrives, not how much it costs when it does. Lesson 72.

title: Four positions, how many bets
description: The divisor takes a count and an average correlation and returns the truth.
context: You hold four positions. Their average pairwise correlation is 0.85.

options.text: 4.00 bets
2.35 bets
1.13 bets
0.85 bets

explanation: The count divided by one plus the count less one times the average: 4 divided by (1 + 3 times 0.85) is 4 over 3.55, which is 1.13 independent bets. Four positions at that correlation are barely more than one. The ceiling as you keep adding positions is one over the correlation, which here is 1.18. Lesson 71.

title: How long before you know
description: An edge and a bar. How many trades does the verdict take?
context: You believe the edge is 0.15R a trade. The sequential test needs 5.8888 divided by the edge squared.

options.text: 39 trades
262 trades
589 trades
1,047 trades

explanation: 5.8888 divided by 0.15 squared is 5.8888 over 0.0225, which is 262 trades. Note how fast this moves: the same test on an edge of a tenth of an R needs 589, because the count goes as one over the edge squared. Halve the edge and you quadruple the wait. Lesson 67.

title: What the depth costs in the account
description: A drawdown in R, and a risk per trade. What is it in per cent?
context: The median worst drawdown for an edge like yours is 8.82R. You risk one and a half per cent a trade.

options.text: 8.82 per cent of the account
13.23 per cent
5.88 per cent
1.50 per cent

explanation: 8.82 times 1.5 per cent is 13.23 per cent of the account. R is a unit of risk, so converting a depth in R to a depth in money is one multiplication, and it is the multiplication that decides whether you can sit through the drawdown you should expect. Lesson 67, sized by lesson 20.

title: What the point of control is
description: The busiest price of the session. How stable is it?
context: You read the point of control off a volume profile and plan to trade against it.

options.text: A price the market is drawn back to
The mode of a binned distribution, which moves with the bin width
The session VWAP under another name
The midpoint of the value area

explanation: It is the mode of a distribution you binned, and a mode is the summary a bin width moves most: lesson 29 measures it sliding 9.5 ticks across a 15-tick day purely by changing the setting. Nothing in the course establishes it as a level price returns to. The value area is the steadier reading, at 3.5 ticks of movement.

title: Count the places before the signals
description: A swing rule decides how much there is to find before an indicator is consulted.
context: On sixty closes, marking swings at one bar either side gives 33 places to look. Marking at three bars either side gives 5.

options.text: The looser rule finds better signals
The looser rule grants itself 6.6 times the opportunities
The two rules will agree on most signals
The difference only matters for divergence

explanation: 33 divided by 5 is 6.6. Before either setting has looked at an oscillator it has already decided how many chances it gets, and the looser one gets six and a half times as many. That is a search width, and lesson 64 prices what search width does to a result. Lesson 34.

title: Three settings, three answers
description: The same sixty bars, and a word two people are using differently.
context: Which levels count, whether a wick past is enough or the close has to stay inside, and how soon back inside still counts.

options.text: The settings barely change the count
Ordinary values of the three find 4 sweeps, or 15, or 46
Only the level rule matters
A sweep is defined by the exchange

explanation: On lesson 35’s sixty bars, ordinary values of those three settings find four sweeps, or fifteen, or forty-six. The middle pile, closed beyond but back within two bars, is the entire disagreement between two people who both think they are using the same word.

title: What confirmation buys
description: Deciding a regime has just changed is a trade between lag and false alarms.
context: On sixty closes a detector run with no confirmation declares 8 changes. You add one bar of confirmation, then five.

options.text: 8, then 7, then 6
8, then 4, then 2
8, then 8, then 8
The count rises with confirmation

explanation: One bar of confirmation halves the declared changes from eight to four and five bars halves it again to two. The part that surprises people is the other column: how much of the move you end up inside does not fall as you add confirmation. It goes seven, four, three, two, and then ten out of ten. Lesson 37.

title: The unit that moved
description: Everything after lesson 63 is quoted in R. What happens when R is measured twice?
context: One bar’s dispersion is 2.0446 on the first half of a record and 0.7543 on the second. A t-statistic on the same record reads 3.65.

options.text: The t falls to 1.35
The t rises to 9.89
The t is unchanged at 3.65
The t cannot be computed

explanation: A t is a mean over a standard error and both are in the same units, so a constant divisor cancels exactly: 3.65 in dollars is 3.65 in R and 3.65 in either half’s R. Every ratio survives. What does not survive is every distance: the unit moved by a factor of 2.711 between the halves, so an eight-R line is two different distances wearing one name. Lesson 85.

title: Is the third chart a second witness
description: Three widths of the same tape, and what agreement is worth.
context: You require three timeframes to agree before taking a trade. On forty bars, all three call a trend on seven of them.

options.text: Agreement proves the signal
Compare the observed agreement against what unrelated series would give
Three charts are always better than one
The widest chart should decide

explanation: A wider chart is the same tape regrouped, not a second source, so agreement is expected even with no information in it. Work out what unrelated series would give: multiply the two yes rates, add the product of the two no rates. If your observed agreement is not comfortably above that, the third chart is not a witness. Lesson 39.

title: What the footprint decides
description: Two bars, identical in every printed field but one.
context: Two bars share their open, high, low, close, total volume and even the volume traded at every individual price. Their deltas are +2,820 and −1,680.

options.text: The negative-delta bar is absorption and should be bought
The negative-delta bar is exhaustion and should be faded
Both readings are taught, both are consistent, and the footprint does not decide between them
The bars cannot both be real

explanation: One school calls it absorption and buys, the other calls it exhaustion and fades. Both are internally consistent and the chart contains nothing that separates them. Before either reading is worth arguing about, find out whether your delta is published by the venue or inferred by your software, and get the base rate: how often price and delta disagree at all. Lesson 28.

title: What the spread is paying for
description: The market maker quotes both sides. What does the spread have to cover?
context: You are working out why a spread is the width it is.

options.text: The venue’s profit margin
Inventory risk, adverse selection and the fee schedule
Volatility alone
Whatever the market maker can get away with

explanation: Three things: carrying inventory it did not choose, the cost of being adversely selected because the orders that hit a resting quote are more likely to know something, and the fee schedule it trades under. That is why the spread widens when the chance of an informed counterparty rises, rather than because someone decided to charge more. Lesson 53.

title: What doubling the size costs
description: Impact does not scale the way the spread does.
context: Your order moves the price against you. Impact grows roughly as size to the power of one and a half.

options.text: Doubling the size doubles the impact
Doubling the size multiplies the impact by 2.83
Doubling the size quadruples the impact
Impact does not depend on size

explanation: Two to the power of one and a half is 2.83. The spread and the commission are linear in size and the impact is not, which is why a rule that works small can stop working large and why there is a crossover size beyond which impact is the whole bill. Lesson 59, and lesson 68 turns it into a capacity.

title: The part a second venue cannot reach
description: A round trip split into what it is actually made of.
context: A round trip costs 0.1230 a share: a penny of spread, 0.1030 of slippage, and a cent of commission.

options.text: Slippage is 8.1 per cent of the bill
Slippage is 50 per cent of the bill
Slippage is 83.7 per cent of the bill
The three parts are roughly equal

explanation: 0.1030 divided by 0.1230 is 83.7 per cent. A second venue competes for the spread and the commission, which is 0.0200 of 0.1230 or 16.3 per cent, and it cannot touch the rest: slippage is a delay, and a delay does not care where the order is sent. Lesson 83.

title: The field the tape never carries
description: An off-exchange print is public the moment it is done. What is missing?
context: The tape gives the price, the size and the fact that it happened away from an exchange, within ten seconds.

options.text: The time
The side: nobody on the tape is marked as the buyer
The venue fee
Nothing is missing

explanation: The side is never carried. The rule the folklore uses to fill it in, above the running volume-weighted average is accumulation and below it is distribution, fills it in with the day’s price path instead, because a running average is made of the prices behind it. On the curriculum’s own sixty closes the accumulation share tracks the session return at a correlation of 0.93. Lesson 56.

title: The cost of checking
description: The same record, judged two ways.
context: A 156-trade record judged once at the end lets a system with no edge pass 5.05 per cent of the time. Now judge after every trade from trade 20 and stop the first time it clears the bar.

options.text: It still passes about 5 per cent of the time
It passes 24.25 per cent of the time, 4.80 times as often
It passes about 10 per cent of the time
Checking early cannot change the result

explanation: 24.25 divided by 5.05 is 4.80. Nothing about the system changed and nothing about the market changed. What changed is how many chances you gave a dead system to look alive, and the fix costs nothing: write the horizon down before the first trade. Lesson 65.

title: What the line switches off
description: A drawdown limit protects you from something and costs you something else.
context: You will switch a system off if it draws down eight R.

options.text: It removes almost no genuine systems
It removes about a quarter of genuine systems
It removes 59.5 per cent of the systems that genuinely work
It only removes systems with no edge

explanation: An eight-R line switches off 59.5 per cent of the systems that genuinely work, because a real edge spends a lot of its life underwater. The number to write down before you start is the depth you will sit through, and lesson 67 gives you the depth you should expect rather than the one that feels tolerable in the moment.

title: Two habits, compounded
description: Not the cost of one habit. The cost of two.
context: A hundred candidate rules of which one in ten is genuinely alive. Judged once, 43.2 per cent of what the test accepts is real. Now peek, and abandon at eight R.

options.text: About 35 per cent is still real
About 20 per cent is still real
6.0 per cent is real, and you accept nearly three times as many rules
The share is unchanged; only the count rises

explanation: You end up accepting 23.2 rules rather than 8.0, of which 1.40 are real instead of 3.46. Nearly three times as many systems and two fifths as many true ones. The habits do not cost you money directly; they cost you the meaning of the word yes, and they cost most where good rules are rarest, which is exactly where a person who has not found one yet is standing. Lesson 84.

title: The bar and the record
description: Three lessons ask for a trade count and each names a different one.
context: The book you have has seven trades. Lesson 65 fixes a horizon of 156 before the first trade, lesson 67 wants 589, and a quarter-wage cost base wants 1,047.

options.text: Aim for the largest, since it is the most rigorous
The fixed horizon at 22.3 times the record is the reachable one
Seven trades is enough if the t-statistic is high
The three numbers are interchangeable

explanation: At 56.5 round trips a year those four are 0.12, 2.76, 10.42 and 18.53 years, which is 1, 22.3, 84.1 and 149.6 times the record you have. Two years and nine months of trading the rule you already own is a plan; a decade is not, and a working life is not. And it is reachable precisely because it was fixed before the first trade rather than demanded after it. Lesson 81.
